question: What causes compass deviation?

options.text: The aircraft's own magnetism
Magnetic dip at high latitudes
The difference between true and magnetic north
The rotation of the Earth

explanation: Iron and steel in the airframe and engines, and electrical currents, create fields that deflect the compass. Variation, the true-to-magnetic difference, is a property of the Earth, not the aircraft.

question: How is compass heading converted to magnetic heading?

options.text: Magnetic heading = true heading + deviation
Magnetic heading = compass heading + deviation
Magnetic heading = compass heading + variation
Magnetic heading = compass heading − deviation

explanation: Easterly deviation is added and westerly deviation subtracted ("deviation east, compass least"). Variation is then applied to obtain true heading.

question: On a heading of 090° magnetic, the deviation is 4° east. What does the compass read?
explanation: Compass = magnetic − easterly deviation = 090 − 4 = 086°. With easterly deviation the compass reads least.

question: The compass reads 272° and the deviation on that heading is 3° W. What is the magnetic heading?
explanation: Magnetic = compass + deviation, with west negative: 272 − 3 = 269°. "Deviation west, compass best": the compass reads more than magnetic.

question: Which of these affect a direct reading compass in the aircraft?

options.text: Plastic fittings and electrical equipment
Ferrous metals and electrical equipment
Non-ferrous metals only
Ferrous metals only

explanation: Iron and steel parts, magnetised or magnetisable, and the magnetic fields of electrical currents both cause deviation. Non-ferrous metals such as aluminium have no effect.

question: True heading is 247°, variation 8°W and deviation 11°E. What is the compass heading?
explanation: Magnetic heading = true + westerly variation = 247 + 8 = 255°. Compass heading = magnetic − easterly deviation = 255 − 11 = 244°. Adding the deviation gives the 266° slip.

question: In aircraft magnetism, what is "hard iron" magnetism?

options.text: Magnetism found only in aluminium alloys
Magnetism induced by the Earth's field that varies with heading
Permanent magnetism in the airframe structure
Magnetism from the Earth's field at the magnetic poles

explanation: Hard iron is magnetised during manufacture and stays so. Its field is fixed relative to the aircraft, so its effect on the compass changes as the aircraft changes heading.

question: How is the permanent (hard iron) magnetism of an aircraft resolved for analysis?

options.text: Into two components: horizontal H and vertical Z
Into one total field T
Into coefficients A, B and C only
Into P, Q and R

explanation: P acts along the longitudinal axis, Q along the lateral axis and R along the vertical axis. P and Q give the heading-dependent deviations that a swing corrects.

question: A hard iron component acts fore and aft along the aircraft. On which headings does it cause maximum deviation?

options.text: It causes the same deviation on all headings
North and south
East and west

explanation: On east or west, the fore-and-aft field is at right angles to the Earth's horizontal field and deflects the magnets most. On north or south it lies along the field and causes none. The deviation varies as the sine of the heading.

question: A hard iron component acts athwartships. How does the deviation it causes vary with heading?

options.text: As cos heading
It is zero on all headings
It is constant on all headings
As the sine of heading, maximum on east and west

explanation: The lateral field is at right angles to H on north and south, giving maximum deviation there, and in line with it on east and west. This is coefficient C.

question: Why is the vertical hard iron component R usually ignored in a compass swing?

options.text: It is always cancelled by soft iron
It only affects the compass when the aircraft is not level
It is removed by the pendulous suspension
It only exists in the southern hemisphere

explanation: A vertical field has no horizontal effect while the aircraft is level, which is how the swing is carried out. It matters when the aircraft pitches or banks.

question: What is "soft iron" magnetism in an aircraft?

options.text: Magnetism in the compass liquid
Permanent magnetism created during manufacture
Magnetism found only in the compass magnets
Temporary magnetism induced by the Earth's field

explanation: Soft iron in the aircraft becomes magnetised by the Earth's field it sits in. Its strength and direction change with heading and with magnetic latitude.

question: Why does deviation due to soft iron change when the aircraft moves to a new magnetic latitude?

options.text: The compass liquid changes density
The aircraft's hard iron changes with latitude
The inducing field changes with latitude
Soft iron loses its magnetism over time

explanation: Induced magnetism depends on the field causing it. As H and Z change with latitude, so does the soft iron magnetism and the deviation it produces. A big change of latitude is one reason to re-swing.

question: What is coefficient A?

options.text: The deviation on north only
The same deviation on all headings
A deviation varying with the sine of heading
A deviation varying with the cosine of heading

explanation: Coefficient A is usually mechanical, from a misaligned lubber line or compass. It is corrected by loosening the compass, or a remote compass's detector unit, and turning it.

question: How is coefficient A corrected?

options.text: By moving the latitude nut
By adjusting the compass's magnetic corrector on east or west
By adjusting the corrector on north or south
By loosening the compass or detector unit and rotating it

explanation: Since coefficient A is a fixed angular offset, rotating the unit to align its lubber line removes it.

question: What is coefficient B?

options.text: Deviation varying as the sine of heading, greatest on east and west
Deviation varying as the cosine of heading, greatest on north and south
Deviation caused by the vertical component R
A constant deviation on all headings

explanation: Coefficient B comes mainly from fore-and-aft magnetism. It is calculated and corrected on an easterly or westerly heading.

question: What is coefficient C?

options.text: A constant deviation on all headings
Deviation varying as cos heading
Deviation varying as the sine of heading, greatest on east and west
Deviation caused by the lubber line being misaligned

explanation: Coefficient C comes mainly from athwartships magnetism. It is calculated and corrected on a northerly or southerly heading.

question: On which heading is coefficient B corrected during a compass swing?

options.text: Any intercardinal heading
A northerly or southerly heading
An easterly or westerly heading
North only

explanation: B is greatest on east and west, where its effect can be isolated and removed. C is corrected on north or south.

question: During a compass swing the deviations are: N +3°, E +5°, S −1°, W −1°. What is coefficient B?
explanation: B = (deviation on E − deviation on W) ÷ 2 = (5 − (−1)) ÷ 2 = +3°. Forgetting to halve gives +6°.

question: Using the same deviations, N +3°, E +5°, S −1°, W −1°, what is coefficient C?
explanation: C = (deviation on N − deviation on S) ÷ 2 = (3 − (−1)) ÷ 2 = +2°.

question: Using the same deviations, N +3°, E +5°, S −1°, W −1°, what is coefficient A?
explanation: A is the mean deviation: (3 + 5 − 1 − 1) ÷ 4 = +1.5°. It is the part that does not change with heading.

question: After a compass swing and correction, how is the remaining deviation found?

options.text: By a check swing
By calculation from the coefficients only
By a single check on north
By comparing with the DGI in flight

explanation: The check swing measures the residual deviations, which are put on a compass deviation card or shown as a curve. The card is placed near the compass.

question: After correction, what is the maximum deviation allowed for a direct reading magnetic compass under the operating rules?
explanation: A direct reading compass must be within ±10°. A remote indicating compass, which is used for precise navigation, must be within ±1°.

question: After correction, what is the maximum deviation allowed for a remote indicating compass under the operating rules?
explanation: The remote compass is the primary heading source on large aircraft, so the limit is much tighter than the ±10° allowed for the standby direct reading compass.

question: Which of these is a reason to swing the compass?

options.text: After every flight
After refuelling
After a lightning strike
Before every flight in the southern hemisphere

explanation: Lightning can change the aircraft's magnetism. A swing is also due after installing compass parts, doubtful accuracy, major modifications, shocks, a move to a very different magnetic latitude and long storage on one heading.

question: Why may an aircraft need a compass swing after long-term storage on one heading?

options.text: Its hard iron magnetism may change
Variation will have changed
The compass magnets will have become weaker
The compass liquid will have evaporated

explanation: Standing on one heading for a long time, the airframe can pick up magnetism from the Earth's field. Vibration and hammering during maintenance do the same.

question: Why may a compass swing be needed when an aircraft moves to a new theatre of operations?

options.text: The compass is affected by the new climate
The soft iron deviation changes with the new latitude
The new country may use a different heading reference
Variation is different there

explanation: Soft iron magnetism is induced by the local Earth field, which changes with magnetic latitude. A large move therefore changes the deviation.

question: Which of these would NOT normally require a compass swing?

options.text: Fitting new radio or electrical equipment
Replacing the compass
A significant repair involving magnetic material
Changing the engine oil

explanation: Changes to electrical systems, compass components or magnetic structure all alter deviation. Routine servicing that does not change the aircraft's magnetic properties does not.
